title: Morning light over La Silla
caption: The New Technology Telescope and the ESO 3.6-meter telescope under the Milky Way, La Silla Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at La Silla Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: With the Milky Way as a backdrop, two telescopes crown a hill at the center of this view of ESO's La Silla Observatory. The rectangular building on the left houses the New Technology Telescope (NTT), and the dome on the right belongs to the ESO 3.6-meter telescope. Set up in the 1960s, La Silla was the first observatory ESO built in Chile.

The 3.58-meter NTT opened in 1989 as the world's first telescope with a computer-controlled main mirror. That mirror is flexible, and during observations its shape is continually adjusted to keep images as sharp as possible. The technique, called active optics, is now used on all major modern telescopes, among them the future European Extremely Large Telescope and the Very Large Telescope on Cerro Paranal.
Other telescopes share the site, including the Swedish–ESO Submillimeter Telescope (SEST) and TAROT, a robotic instrument that watches for fast-changing events such as gamma-ray bursts.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph by José Joaquín Pérez. The source does not publish camera, exposure or color-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the Milky Way may appear brighter and more detailed here than to someone standing on the site.

explore: The photographer, ESO Photo Ambassador José Joaquín Pérez, works as an agricultural engineer when he is not photographing the night sky, devoting his time to protecting crops in central Chile.
